questions.stem: A checkout service runs on a VM where availableProcessors() returns 8, started with no pool-related JVM flags. A request thread runs `orders.parallelStream().map(this::score).toList()` over 500,000 orders while nothing else in the JVM runs parallel work. Which threads can run score()?

options.text: The pool's seven workers only, since the request thread just waits for their results
options.says: the caller runs pieces of the work itself instead of waiting

options.text: The pool's eight workers plus the request thread, since the caller takes pieces of the work too
options.says: the common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 workers, seven here, not eight

options.text: The pool's seven workers plus the request thread, since the caller takes pieces of the work too
options.says: the common pool's parallelism defaults to availableProcessors() - 1, and the thread that calls the terminal operation works like one more worker

options.text: The pool's eight workers only, since the request thread just waits for their results
options.says: the common pool has availableProcessors() - 1 workers, and the caller runs pieces itself

origin.section: A Parallel Stream Runs on the Common ForkJoinPool, With Its Caller as One More Worker

questions.stem: An order service on a 16-CPU machine runs a nightly export, `customers.parallelStream().map(crm::fetchProfile).toList()`, where each fetchProfile() waits two to three seconds on an HTTP call. While the export runs, the notification code calls `CompletableFuture.runAsync(this::sendEmail)` with no executor. What happens to those emails during the export?

options.text: They wait, since runAsync tasks queue behind the export until its terminal operation ends
options.says: nothing reserves the pool for the stream; the tasks wait because every worker is blocked in a call, and a worker that comes back can run them

options.text: They wait, since the pool's workers are all inside fetchProfile() and none is added in their place
options.says: default async tasks run on the common pool, its workers stay busy while they wait in fetchProfile, and the pool starts no thread in their place

options.text: They go out at once, since the pool adds a worker in place of each one that is inside fetchProfile()
options.says: the pool starts no thread in place of a worker blocked in I/O; its javadoc promises no such adjustment

options.text: They go out at once, since runAsync gives a task a thread of its own when the pool is busy
options.says: runAsync without an executor falls back to a thread per task only when the pool's parallelism is below two, not when it is busy

origin.section: A Blocking Call Inside a Parallel Stream Starves Every Other User of the Common Pool

questions.stem: A batch job keeps three million sensor readings in a LinkedList<Reading> and sums one field of each, a few arithmetic operations per reading. On a 32-core machine the team changes stream() to parallelStream(). What are they likely to see?

options.text: Little gain, since a parallel stream over a List stays on the calling thread unless the list is an ArrayList
options.says: a parallel stream over any List runs on the common pool; how well it splits depends on the list's spliterator

options.text: A large gain, since the list can be cut into equal pieces for the workers before any summing starts
options.says: the pieces come from trySplit, and a LinkedList can't hand out halves without walking to them

options.text: A large gain, since a parallel stream over a List spreads it over all 32 cores whatever kind of list it is
options.says: the kind of list decides how well it splits; with cheap work the linked list gained 10 % or nothing

options.text: Little gain, since the list can only be cut into pieces by walking it on one thread
options.says: a LinkedList splits by copying batches of 1024, 2048, ... elements on the splitting thread; with cheap work that walk dominates

origin.section: The Source Decides How Well the Work Splits

questions.stem: A request handler totals the 300 line items of a cart with `items.parallelStream().mapToLong(Item::cents).sum()` on a 16-core server, thousands of times a second. `items` is an ArrayList. Compared with stream(), what does each call cost?

options.text: More time, since creating tasks and handing them to the workers costs more than 300 additions
options.says: a parallel run pays a fixed price of tens to hundreds of microseconds; 300 additions take far less

options.text: More time, since the 300 items are copied into an array before the stream splits them
options.says: an ArrayList splits by index into halves without copying

options.text: Less time, since the 300 items are split into sixteen slices that are added at once
options.says: the fixed price of a parallel run outweighs the share of 300 additions each thread saves

options.text: Less time, since handing tasks to workers that are already started costs less than 300 additions
options.says: creating, handing off, waking and joining tasks still costs tens to hundreds of microseconds per run

origin.section: Parallel Pays Only When the Work Outweighs Splitting and Merging

questions.stem: A fraud job runs `txIds.parallelStream().unordered().filter(this::suspicious).limit(100).toList()` over an ArrayList of ten million transaction ids in time order. Which suspicious ids does it return?

options.text: 100 ids from near the end of the list, since limit after unordered() keeps the ones the threads find last
options.says: limit after unordered() keeps any matches, from wherever threads find them, not the last ones

options.text: The first 100 ids in list order, since an ArrayList source keeps its order through unordered()
options.says: after unordered() the parallel limit returned elements from the middle of the list instead of the first ones

options.text: 100 ids from anywhere in the list, since limit after unordered() keeps whichever ones the threads find
options.says: after unordered() any n matches will do; the parallel limit returned matches from the middle of the list

options.text: The first 100 ids in list order, since toList() puts the ids back in list order at the end
options.says: toList() can only keep the order the stream still has; after unordered() limit has already chosen elements without regard to it
